text: Breaking today: 42AI emerges with a model designed to
predict human behavior.
From the SanMitra Newsroom,
this is the Daily AI Brief for 09 November 2026.
Our lead story today.
An Israeli-American startup called 42AI has made its
public debut, TechCrunch reported on 2 November.
The company says its system,
which it calls a behavioral world model,
can estimate how people will react when they face
situations they have not met before.
Financial brokerages are its first market.
The startup has disclosed 62.5 million dollars in seed
funding.
That money came from its founders and Infinity Group
over three years, not in one new round.
Its predictive performance is so far only the company's
own claim.
The widely quoted figure of 98% accuracy measures
whether trading flows land within a range.
It does not mean every trade is predicted correctly.
Turning to the United States.
Fal, a company that hosts video,
image and audio models,
has raised 1.3 billion dollars in a Series F round,
TechCrunch reported on 3 November.
Bessemer Venture Partners led the round,
which reportedly values Fal at 16 billion dollars ,
twice its valuation in April.
Fal disclosed its Series E and Series F at the same
time, for a combined 1.65 billion dollars .
That total includes the 1.3 billion dollars rather than
adding to it.
The deal points to investors moving money toward the
business of running AI models for customers.
Even so, the high cost of computing continues to put
pressure on the profit margins of these inference
providers.
In other news.
The US Justice Department announced on 5 November what
it calls a Super Intelligence Task Force.
The unit will coordinate enforcement against illegal
uses of artificial intelligence by foreign actors,
criminal groups and companies.
According to Nextgov, it absorbs the department's
earlier AI litigation task force and will draw up
guidance on prosecutions and compliance.
While the public announcement came this week,
the memorandum behind it is dated 13 October.
The phrase super intelligence reflects the
administration's own choice of words.
It does not indicate that artificial intelligence
surpassing humans across the board has been achieved.
In Asia.
Google announced on 3 November that it is broadening its
academic partnerships in Singapore with more than 6
million dollars in support for research and capacity
building, alongside its recently opened research hub in
the city.
The projects include Alzheimer's research assisted by AI
at NUS, work on computing efficiency and regional
languages, studies on AI safety at NTU,
and backing for INSEAD's Thrive Lab.
These are commitments of funding and planned research,
rather than finished scientific advances.
Turning to India.
Peppermint Robotics, which is based in Pune and Austin,
announced on 4 November that it has raised 100 crore
rupees in a Pre-Series B round.
The round was led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture
Partners, with Asiana Fund also taking part.
The deal combines fresh investment with sales of
existing shares, meaning the business itself will not
receive the full 100 crore rupees .
The company's autonomous cleaning robots rely on
computer vision and LiDAR to map spaces,
plan routes and steer around obstacles.
Peppermint plans to increase manufacturing,
move into cleanroom robotics and set up an assembly line
in North America.
Figures on its deployments and revenue growth are the
company's own claims.
Around the world.
Google is facing criticism from parents and teachers in
the United States over a new condition attached to its
classroom technology, the Guardian reports.
Last week the company released a group of artificial
intelligence tools for schools,
along with settings that let teachers and administrators
limit how those tools are used.
Google says each school can decide for itself whether
students get access to AI.
But there is a condition.
Any school that switches off the AI tools will also lose
access to Google Search.
Chris Phillips, Google's vice-president for education,
defended the policy.
"We believe schools should have control over AI in their
classrooms," he said.
Phillips added that the company sought input from
researchers, policymakers, schools and teachers before
it changed the controls covering Gemini,
Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search.
In other news.
Nvidia, SK Telecom and the chip designer Rebellions plan
to jointly build a hybrid artificial intelligence
computing system for SK Telecom's data centers,
according to the Korea Times.
The three companies signed a memorandum of understanding
on Monday at AI Day Seoul,
a two-day Nvidia event in the south of the city.
Under the arrangement, Rebellions' neural processing
chips will connect to Nvidia's graphics processors
through a program called NVLink Fusion.
The program lets major cloud operators and makers of
custom chips attach their own AI processors to Nvidia's
rack-scale systems.
South Korea's science ministry said the deal could
create new applications for the country's advanced chips
and strengthen the position of Korean companies in
overseas markets.
Nvidia also held a forum that drew more than 20 Korean
startups.
Next.
Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to
hire engineers in Silicon Valley,
Rest of World reports,
a push that could open a path to talent from American
labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
MiniMax, a startup whose shares trade in Hong Kong,
lists roughly 16 vacancies in San Francisco on its
website.
They include a position heading research on its main AI
model.
The company is also seeking experts in life sciences,
law, finance and cybersecurity,
as well as a senior recruiter to attract top AI
engineers from Silicon Valley and Seattle.
Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi model,
is recruiting solutions architects in the United States.
Those staff would help corporate clients build its
models into their businesses.
Success is far from guaranteed.
Turning to the United States.
Google is rolling out two new versions of its own Tensor
Processing Unit chip, Reuters reports.
The first, the 8tx,
is designed for government agencies and regulated
industries, and includes encryption in the hardware
itself to safeguard sensitive information.
The second, the 8i Max,
targets demanding AI workloads such as coding
assistants, mathematical reasoning and drug discovery.
Google is increasingly selling access to its chips
through Google Cloud instead of reserving them for its
own operations.
The move shows that competition in AI now extends beyond
the models themselves.
Command of chips, cloud capacity and computing costs is
growing just as important,
and Google is presenting its processors as an
alternative to Nvidia's hardware.
Also today.
Nvidia said its board of directors has formed an
independent committee, backed by outside lawyers,
to look into reports that chief executive Jensen Huang
may have been the target of a foreign intelligence
operation.
The company said it has no current reason to think that
national security or its own confidential information
was compromised.
Nvidia added that Huang has agreed to fully cooperate
with the inquiry.
Because Nvidia plays a central role in the worldwide AI
supply chain, questions about the security of its
leadership and of access to advanced chips carry weight
far beyond the company.
From the research desk.
The researchers behind a paper titled SplatAnything:
Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS
across Arbitrary Scenes want a widely used 3D modelling
technique to perform more consistently across very
different scenes.
The technique, known as 3D Gaussian splatting,
represents a scene as a large number of small,
blob-like shapes called Gaussians.
In quicker feed-forward versions,
a neural network predicts those shapes in one pass.
The researchers found that existing approaches resize
scenes using one overall distance measure,
yet the spacing between neighbouring Gaussians still
swings widely depending on scene size and camera
placement.
That leaves the network uncertain how big each Gaussian
should be.
Their solution, called GSNorm,
rescales each scene using a robust estimate of that
spacing, giving the network a steadier reference point.
To recap today's top stories.
42AI emerges with a model designed to predict human
behavior.
Fal raises 1.3 billion dollars as demand for AI
inference grows.
US Justice Department announces a consolidated AI
enforcement task force.
Google expands Singapore research with more than 6
million dollars in funding.
Peppermint raises 100 crore rupees to expand autonomous
cleaning robots.
Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search
if schools block AI:
‘This threat is nothing but extortion’.
Those were today's critical developments across global
artificial intelligence.
From our bureaus covering World,
USA, China, Asia, and India,
thank you for watching SanMitra AI News Wire.
